MONK (Jacques Cartier) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 53) respecting Insolvency. He said :	I may say at
once to the House that this is the same Bill that was introduced in 1898 by Mr. Fortin, the former member for Laval, now judge of the Superior Court. At that time I took some interest in the measure, and was a member of the committee that was struck for the purpose of studying it and making a report upon it. I think it would be a pity that the measure should fall, for the reason principally that it was submitted to all the boards of trade of this country, and was approved by them all with the exception of the board of trade of Winnipeg, which for some reason or other refrained from giving the Bill its express approbation. Under these circumstances, the Bill, as framed at that time, met the requirements of all the different provinces of the Dominion. At the present moment there is a great demand for uniform legislation throughout the Dominion on this important subject, and it is with that view that 1 am re-introducing the Bill. I will give further explanations when it comes up for its second reading.

Mr. Speaker, before tlie Orders of the Day are proceeded with, I desire to direct the attention of the House to the present situation in Ontario ; and, in order that I may put myself within the rules of the House, I intend to conclude with a motion. In the Canada ' Gazette ' of Saturday, the following announcement occurs :
Department of the Secretary of State of
Canada.
His Excellency the Governor General has been pleased to make the following appointments. viz.:
March 26, 1903.
The Honourable Charles Moss, Chief Justice of Ontario, to be the administrator of the province of Ontario for the purpose of assenting to such bills as may be required during the present session of the legislature of Ontario, of assenting to the Bills passed by such legislature at the close of the session ; and of proroguing the present session of the legislative assembly of Ontario.
I take this opportunity of asking the right lion, gentleman who leads the House to state to whom has been assigned the other high duties that are attached to the office of Lieutenant Governor of Ontario. The Lieutenant Governor of Ontario, like all other lieutenant governors, exercises other prerogatives of the Crown than those mentioned in the ' Gazette,' and so far as we know, they are left to some one else. Now, I believe that the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario is very ill, and somebody must be discharging those other duties. Let me point out from one of the authorities what is included in the other duties of the lieutenaut governor. At page 30 of 'Confederation Law of Canada,' by Wheeler, it is stated :
The Executive Council of Ontario and of Quebec shall be composed of such persons as the Lieutenant Governor from time to time thinks fit.
and so on. A serious political crisis exists in the province of Ontario ; grave charges have been made against ministers of the Crown and are now under discussion in the Ontario legislature ; and in view of the fact that the government have confessed that the lieutenant governor is unable to discharge three of his duties, and have appointed somebody else to discharge them, I want to know who is discharging these other duties, and passing upon the fitness of the ministers of the Crown. Let me quote another authority, Mr. Goldwin Smith, who the other day made the following statement :
Mr. Ross, it has always been maintained in these columns, had much better after the general election have met without delay the legislature which he had called, taken a decisive vote, and thereupon made up his mind whether he was in a position to carry on the government. He preferred, as a matter of party tactics, to fight the battle out In tbe elec-

tion courts, and in such by-elections as might ensue. He thereby manifestly exposed the province to a reign of intrigue and corruption, as well as to an extraordinary outburst of party rancour. He now sees the result. It is much worse for him than even a defeat upon an appeal to the legislature would have been. In that case he would at all events have retained the confidence and support of a united party. As it is, he is threatened with total wreck.
I am not raising a political question, but I want to show what Mr. Goldwin Smith's position is. He goes on to say :
The proper arbiter of the course to be taken by the ministers in such circumstances as these is the lieutenant governor. By him the ministers are appointed, and he is responsible to the province for their integrity. It is very unfortunate if, as is stated, he is incapacitated by sickness for the performance of his functions.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have made out that the lieutenant governor has been considered by the Governor in Council here to he incompetent to discharge certain of his functions, and that there are other high functions which require to be discharged at this moment; and I take this opportunity of asking the right hon. First Minister whether these other functions have been assigned to any one. I have not the slightest intention to reflect on his honour the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario. I have the highest respect for him. I am rising here solely from a conception of my public duty. I think I speak for the people of Ontario, for constitutional practice, and for a majority of the members from Ontario of this House, without claiming to speak for them from a party point of view ; and I ask the Prime Minister to tell the House and the country what he is doing in connection with the present serious situation in the province of Ontario. I move that the House do now adjourn.

Some few minutes ago, Mr. Speaker, myi hon. friend sent me word that he intended to bring before the House the condition of the health of his honour the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario. I would have much preferred that my hon. friend had agreed to the suggestion I made in reply, that he would defer doing so until tomorrow, on the motion to go into Committee of Supply. However, for reasons I shall not discuss, he did not see fit to accede to my request. One of the reasons which induced me ^o ask my hon. friend not to bring the question before the House at this moment was that if he had granted me the privilege I asked, I would have written at once to Sir Oliver Mowat for permission to read to the House a letter which I received from him, and which was the cause of the recommendation I made a few days ago to His Excellency to appoint an administrator for certain purposes. In the absence of such permission, there are in this letter some personal matters which I would

not like to bring before the House, but if I may speak of the general tenor of the letter, it was a request for the appointment by His Excellency the Governor General of an administrator, who would give the necessary sanction to certain Bills this session and who would also prorogue parliament. My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) asked me who is administering the other duties of the Lieutenant Governor. It seems to me there was no need for him to put such a question. Sir Oliver Mowat is the Lieutenant Governor of the province, and is administering all the duties of the office except those which he himself has asked to be assigned to another person. The reason why Sir Oliver Mowat asks that an administrator be appointed to give the sanction of the Lieutenant Governor to the Bills passed during the session and prorogue the session, which is not expected to last very long, is that he has been incapacitated by an accident, which he met with some days ago, which confines him to his room. Otherwise he is in good health and qui^e able to discharge, and is now discharging, the duties of his office. My hon. friend says that Sir Oliver Mowat is not able to discharge the duties of his office, that his health has incapacitated him from doing so. That is the language which my hon. friend used a moment ago, and I suppose he still stands by it. Well, I have the word of Sir Oliver Mowat himself, for whom my hon. friend says he has very great respect, that he is quite able to discharge all the duties of his office except those I have stated, and the inability to perform which is due solely to physical incapacity. Sir Oliver says that he is otherwise in good health. My hon. friend has told us that- and; in this he voiced the opinion not only of the people of Ontario but of every Canadian that he has the greatest respect for Sir Oliver Mowat. We all have the same respect and when a man of the authority of Sir Oliver Mowat, when a man who commends to such a high degree the respect, confidence and admiration of the whole com munity, says he is quite able to administer all the duties of the office, it seems to me my hon. friend has in that statement an answer to the doubt he has expressed, and ought not to go any further, if indeed he has the respect for Sir Oliver Mowat which he professes to have. It seems to me that my hon. friend ought not to insist that Sir Oliver Mowat is not able to discharge the duties of his office, when he has the assurance of Sir Oliver himself that he considers himself quite able in every respect to discharge all the duties of his office except those which call for such physical exercise as to require him to move from one place to another.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (lit. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Might I ask the date of that letter ?

I really do not recollect, but it is within the last ten days. I am sorry that I have not the privilege of
bringing it to the attention of the House, but if I remember aright, it was written within the past ten days. Under the circumstances what more can be said ? Sir Oliver Mowat had, a fall on the stairs which injured his leg so that he cannot walk, and is therefore not in a condition to go to the House and sanction Bills or prorogue the House. That is why we appointed an administrator. Let me go further. This is the third time this matter lias been brought to the attention of the House. Sir Oliver Mowat is Lieutenant Governor by virtue of the commission issued to him on the proper authority, that of the Dominion government. He can be removed to-day at will, but until last November he could not be removed except for cause. Had we renewed his commission, he would be in the same position. My hon. friend need not go far back for a precedent to which no objection was taken. Some few years ago, we objected to lieutenant governors being kept in office year after year without any renewal of their commissions, but no fault waS ever found when a lieutenant governor was kept in office for some months longer than his actual term. Some few years ago, the late Sir Geocge Kirkpatrick was appointed Lieutenant Governor of Ontario. He was sworn in on the 13th of May, 1892, and his five years term expired on the 13th of May, 1897. But he remained in office during the term of his natural life, or some six or seven months after his commission had expired. He was in very poor health, had undergone an operation, and it was well known he could not live much longer, but we did not chose to disturb him and left him in the enjoyment of the office which he held with the concurrence and respect of everybody in the province of Ontario. I would like to know why a different rule should be applied to Sir Oliver Mowat. Does he not enjoy to as high an extent the confidence of the people of Ontario as did his predecessor ? For all these reasons it seems to me that my hon. friend is not playing the best part he could. If I judge rightly the trend of public opinion, I am warranted in saying that if there is a man in whom the people of Ontario, at this moment have confidence to guide them through the political crisis there existing, it is the man who has for so many years enjoyed to the fullest extent the confidence of that province.

This side of the House, Mr. Speaker, as well as the other side, are extremely gratified to learn that the only reason for the appointment of an administrator for the province of Ontario are those assigned in the Canada * Gazette.' If an administrator be required on account of the physical condition of his honour the Lieutenant Governor, the government were perfectly justified in acceding to Sir Oliver Mowat's request. We are all glad to learn from the right hon. gentleman that the alarming reports as to the mental

and physical condition of his honour are incorrect and that he is only suffering at present from the physical disabilities which require the appointment of an administrator.

I have just heard my right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) say that my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) is playing a part in the representations he has thought fit to make to the House and the government. Well, I have listened to my hon. friend from East York each time he has referred to this matter, and I am not aware of any remark he has made that would justify the right hon leader of the House in claiming that in the language used by my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) there was the slightest tinge of disrespect to the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario. He took occasion to call attention to the inability of the Lieutenant Governor to fulfil the functions of his office at the present moment. On the last occasion, the Prime Minister contended that there was no such inability. But, as a matter of fact, all the remarks of my hon. friend from East York have been fully justified by the Order in Council which appeared in the Canada ' Gazette ' last Saturday. What the hon. gentleman stated was absolutely true ; it is impossible for the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario, at this moment to fulfil some of the functions assigned to him, as shown by the fact that it has been found necessary to assign those functions to somebody else. Thus the stand taken by my hon. friend from East York is amply justified. What I wished particularly to point out, is this-that there seems to be, in my humble estimation, a mistake in this Order in Council. The government, if it had any authority for it's action, must find that authority in section 67 of the Confederation Act, which says :
The Governor General in Council may from time to time appoint an administrator to execute the office and functions as lieutenant governor during his absence, illness, or other inability.
Now, what I submit to you, Sir, is this- that under that section, which must be construed strictly, the only thing which the Governor General of the Dominion can do is to appoint some one to fulfil the office of lieutenant governor. This gives pertinence to the remarks of my hon. friend from East York. It is within the power of this government to appoint somebody to fulfil the office of lieutenant governor entirely, and I question very much if, having complied with that section, the lieutenant governor himself can proceed in the execution of any of the duties assigned to him. Once the government of the Dominion has judged that there is in the case of a lieutenant governor, illness, absence, or other inability, this government may appoint some body to fulfil the office; but nobody, I think, will contend that it was possible for this government to appoint somebody under Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
this section 67, which is the only one that applies, somebody, for instance, with power to dissolve the local legislature, of or somebody with power merely to give assent to Bills or to prorogue the legislature. Now, in this Order in Council, as I read it, there is an appointment made, not of somebody to fulfil the office of lieutenant governor in conformity of the terms of section 67, on account of the illness of the lieutenant governor, but there is only the appointment of somebody for the purpose of giving assent to Bills during the present session, of giving assent to Bills at the close of the session, and of proroguing of the present session. So that, really, the act of this government amounts to this-that the office of lieutenant governor is divided. There is a fragmentary authority left in the hands of the lieutenant governor and power is given to the chief justice to fulfil some of the functions of the lieutenant governor. I have not given the matter very careful consideration, but I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to this House that this action is, ultra vires of the government of the Dominion. The only power they have is, in three specified cases mentioned in section 67, to vest, so to speak the office of lieutenant governor in some other person. But they cannot give to another person a portion of the authority of the lieutenant governor and leave him with his other attributes. I think ample authority can be found for that; and I think it is clear, at first sight, that this government has exercised a power which it has not.

If I may be permitted, the point taken by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) is one in which, I am bound to say there is some reason. But we were guided by the precedent created by Sir John Abbott in the case of Sir Alexander Campbell, who was incapacitated from performing certain duties. After communications between Sir John Abbott and Sir Oliver Mowat, then Prime Minister of Ontario, certain powers were given to administrators for certain limited purposes. We followed that precedent.

With the indulgence of the House, I would say that I think my right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is mistaken with regard to the case of Sir Alexander Campbell. In that case a very singular thing occurred ; a deputy was appointed by the provincial government. If the House will allow me, I will quote from Clement's Canadian Constitution, which says :
During the last illness of the late Lieutenant Governor Campbell, an Order in Council was passed appointing a deputy Lieutenant Governor, and this action on the part of the provincial government gave rise to considerable discussion. It is understood that the Attorney General of Ontario prepared a ' state paper ' in support of this action of his government, but this we have not seen. A lieutenant governor standing, as he does in the same relation

to the government of a province as the Governor General does in relation to the government of the Dominion-has vested in him the appointment of all subordinate executive officers throughout the province, hut we do not see how this could extend to authorize the appointment of a deputy.
The action of the Ontario government in the case of Sir Alexander Campbell has been criticised by all writers on our constitution. They question-and I think with a great deal of right-the power of the provincial government to appoint a deputy to the lieutenant governor, who is an officer of this government.

I think my kon. friend's information is somewhat imperfect. Clement does not go far enough. He had not the facts before him when he made that note on section 67. This debate illustrates the inconvenience of springing questions of this kind on the House without notice. Speaking from memory, I think the deputy to Sir Alexander Campbell was appointed by the local authorities. Sir Oliver Mowat expressed approval of this course. Then the authorities here proceeded as we proceeded. That is, application was made to the federal government, and they did with respect to Sir Alexander Campbell what we did with respect to Sir Oliver Mowat-they confirmed the appointment. And that confirmation was given under the advice of, and after correspondence had been exchanged with, Sir Oliver Mowat, then premier of Ontario. And that is the precedent we have followed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: May I ask if there was an official act of the federal government in that case ?
Yes, an Order in Council passed.
There was a commission issued to this person who took the place of Sir Alexander Campbell-a commission issued in the name of the local government.
I have sent for the papers and will have them here in a few minutes.

Section 67 of the British North America Act taken by itself, seems to be reasonably clear :
The Governor General in Council may from time to time appoint an administrator to execute the office and functions of lieutenant governor during his absence, illness or other inability.
Taking this section alone, I admit that it is certainly enough to raise a great doubt, at all events, as to whether the government has taken the right position in making this appointment, the meaning of the section apparently being that if the Governor General in Council appoint the lieutenant governor at all, they cannot divide his functions, but must delegate them in their entirety. But I do not think that we are driven to find
the meaning of the British North America Act on this point from this section alone. If we turn to a corresponding section with reference to the Governor General, I think we will see at once the great importance and great probability of the contention of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) in the arguments that he put forward being correct. This section shows just what can be done, and shows that the functions in this case can be divided ; and when you find in the 14th section governing the action of the Governor General that the func: tions can be divided, there is much ground for the argument that the functions in the case of a lieutenant governor cannot be so divided. Section 14 says :
It shall be lawful for the Queen, if Her Majesty thinks fit, to authorize the Governor General from time to time to appoint any person or any persons jointly or severally, to be his deputy or deputies within any part or parts of Canada, and in that capacity to exercise during the pleasure of the Governor General such of the powers, authorities and functions of the Governor General as the Governor General deems it necessary or expedient to assign to him or them, subject to any limitations or directions expressed or given by the Queen ; but the appointment of such a deputy or deputies shall not affect the exercises by the Governor General himself of any power, authority or function.
Here we have expressly provided that the Governor General can appoint a person or persons in any part of Canada to exercise for the time being some or any of the functions of the Governor General, and in that way he reserves to himself the exercise of all the other functions, and in order that there should not be any doubt upon this important matter, it is made still clearer by the concluding part of the section, which provides :
But the appointment of such a deputy or deputies shall not affect the exercises by the Governor General himself of any power, authority or function.
So we see in this marked distinction between the two analogous positions, the cogency of the argument put forward on this side, and I hope the government will recognize, if they have not already done so, the important step they have taken in this matter, and the significance of the position in which they are placed. It has been well said that this is not the only ease in which Sir Oliver *Mowat lias been unable to exercise the functions of lieutenant governor. The government are aware that, speaking in the ordinary way. his term has expired. I am not one of those who are anxious to see that hon. gentleman removed from the position he occupies, and removed for the purpose of replacing him with another hon. gentleman who has long been looking forward to the position as the fruits of his labour. I think the House understands very well that I refer to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright! But there has been an argument put for-

ward by the leader of the government which I think tells the other way. He says that because of a crisis in the history of the province of Ontario, the present is an inopportune time to remove from the office of lieutenant governor a gentleman who has shown such conspicuous ability as Sir Oliver Mowat. I submit that this argument is not well taken; because if it is a fact that the government has had in view another gentleman for that position for a long time, and if it be a fact that Sir Oliver Mowat still retains to a large extent the brilliant faculties which he has possessed in the past, surely it is not a great compliment, coming from the First Minister, to the hon. gentleman who aspires to succeed him, to suggest that it would be dangerous now, when there is a crisis in Ontario, to commit to him the administration of the affairs of the province. I hope I am not carried away by any undue admiration for this hon. gentleman, but I do feel that having regard to his faithful public services in the past, having regard to certain promises made to him, it is a little unkind for the First Minister to suggest that it would be dangerous to put the administration of the affairs of Ontario into his hands.

The First Minister has given us the pleasing assurance that he had a letter from Sir Oliver Mowat to the effect that he was physically and mentally in a fit condition to discharge the high functions of his office. I am not going to dispute that, but I am going to say that if the information be at all correct which has come to us from time to time, it is at variance with the statement of the right hon. gentleman. X desire to remind the House that we have a high medical opinion given with regard to the fiuestion of superannuation, that an individual is not always the best judge of his own mental and physical condition. I merely draw attention to that circumstance, without desiring to argue that there is anything incorrect in the statement of the right lion, gentleman.

I understood the right hon. gentleman to say in reply to a statement made by my hoii. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean), referring to the case of the late Sir George Kirkpatrick, that after the Liberal party came into power they allowed Sir George Kirkpatrick to remain in office until the time of his death. I think I am correct in saying that the' right hon. gentleman overlooked the fact that Sir George Kirkpatrick was not in office at the time of his death.
The commission of Sir George Kirkpatrick expired in the month of May, 1897, and his successor was appointed in November, 1897.

Several months after Sir George died. Besides, there was no crisis Mr. LENNOX.
in Ontario at that time, such as exists at the present time.
Motion negatived.

Now, there are in the county of Jacques Cartier a great number of dairymen, farmers and gardeners who come almost every day, and some of them twice a day, to Montreal. Exception is taken, and rightly so, to the condition of the road between Cote des Neiges and Cartierville. The earnings of the toll-gates are large. Why should this road which is travelled over by a large number of farmers and others, riding or driving on Sundays and week days, who reach C6te des Neiges by way of St. Laurent. why, I say, should this be the most neglected part of the highways under the control of the commission ? Why should other roads which are not so much travelled over, be kept, I do say in perfect order-for our roads are not as a rule properly maintained-but at any rate in better order than that road which leads from Montreal to St. Laurent ? If we had some effective legislation, if, for instance, the commissioners were compelled by law to lay before the public yearly a full account of the work carried on, we would find out what are the earnings of that body, and how they expend their revenue. I call the attention of the Finance Minister more particularly to the condition of the road leading to St. Laurent, not only because farmers who live in that neighbourhood have reason to complain, but also because the people of Montreal who have to travel in that direction suffer from the impassable state of the road. I would like to give an instance of the strange way in which the affairs of this board are managed. There is in the county of Jacques Cartier, in the parish of Notre Dame de Graces, situated close to the Lachine canal, a small village called Turcot, inhabited by working people, who, to make a living, have to go to St. Henry, Ste. Cunegonde and Montreal. As a rule, these people cannot get their living in that village. Now, Turcot village, which no doubt the hon. the Prime Minister knows, is hemmed in by turnpikes put up by the commissioners, which are in the way of the people going to their work. The inhabitants of Turcot village, to get to Montreal from the village, or to get to the village from Montreal, travel over but a very small portion of the road maintained by the commissioners. Nevertheless, they are made to pay for using that insignificant bit of road. It is impossible for them to leave their village to go to Montreal, St. Henry or Ste. Cunegonde, without paying the toll. I think that we ought to take the same position to-day. For all ex-

This motion, however, does not deal with the question of exports, but of the expenditure of public money. If this were the public money of the Dominion, my hon. friend's motion would be a proper one, and we would be bound to bring down a return showing how it was expended. As however, it was imperial money, the expenditure of which was made through the friendly offices of a Minister of the Crown, at the request of the imperial government-which request was of course very cheerfully granted-the government of Canada have nothing whatever to do with it. The matter would be a proper one to be brought forward in the parliament of Great Britain but not in this House. But I venture to say that, in treating the opposition in this House-and thus treating the people of Canada-in such a light and jaunty manner as they have done this afternoon, they are making a mistake. If there is any body of men to whom the people as a whole look to for the investigation of matters of this kind, it is necessarily the opposition of the House of Commons, which ever party that opposition may for the time being represent. It is not to be expected that the supporters of the government will be alert to ascertain the position of these matters ns they arise. To whom do the people look ? They look to an alert opposition to investigate these subjects. And I submit, that the Minister of Finance-yes, and the right hon. leader of the government-have not treated the opposition here, and so have not treated the people of the country, with the courtesy that should have been shown on this occasion. Surely that concerns this parliament. Money distributed through the Department of Agriculture, through the officers of the Canadian government, is a matter we have to do with, whether it is our money or not. Supposing, for instance, we gave a grant of public money, as was given by some of the old parliaments before confederation, for a certain purpose, and that money was to be disbursed through the English House of Commons, such as a grant to the families of those who fell in the Crimea, and that thousands of pounds sterling were sent to the British government to be handed to these families, would it be pretended that the government of England would hesitate to give an account on the floor of the House of the way that money had been disbursed, in order that we might see whether the money going through their hands had reached the proper quarters. This is a matter affecting the fair fame of this country ns well as of this government, and the very fact that the government dare not make a simple statement-that could injure no one-if everything was honest and above board-the mere fact that they seek to hide themselves behind the subterfuge that they were disbursing the money of the people of England and not our money, suggests at once that these serious rumours are not merely rumours, and that the belief that many people hold that that money was not disbursed honestly, is well founded. Mr. Speaker, the object of this motion is to call the attention of this House to the proceedings of the interprovincial conference, which was held in the city of Quebec, in December last. This question of readjusting the federal subsidies paid to the provinces under the British North America Act, is apparently coming to a crisis. The present state of affairs call for a solution ; or failing that, the provinces henceforth will have to be satisfied with a less efficient administration of certain departments, to the great detriment of public affairs. Sir, these are growing times and an era Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
of unprecedented prosperity has been ushered in ; now, would it be fair for the provinces, I ask, to keep aloof from that general movement, when the whole world is progressing by leaps and bounds ?
The question of readjusting the Dominion subsidies to provinces is of no recent growth; and it is within the recollection of lion, gentlemen that, on several occasions, this very same question was threshed out in this House, but, I make bold to say here and now, without the least fear of contradiction, that in the province of Quebec, it is a matter which is irrespective of party affiliations.
As early as 1882, the treasurer of the Quebec government urged upon the Dominion authorities the desirability of a more liberal grant being secured by the provinces. In the year 1883, a similar demand for better terms was made by the provincial authorities. In 1884, the late Sir Adolphe Chap-leau brought to bear a pretty strong pressure upon his colleagues in order to engage the then government to take action in the matter and to increase by $250,000 the Dominion grant to the province. As all the hon. gentlemen know, the increase in subsidies applied for was to indemnify the province of Quebec for the considerable outlay it had incurred in building the North Shore Railway, which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had just bought. But it was only in 1887 that the question as to the readjustment of the federal subsidies assumed a more definite shape, through the increasing efforts and the indomitable energy of the late Honore Mercier. All the provinces of confederation, with the exception of British Columbia, then passed resolutions which will go down to history as the most remarkable statement and the most forcible plea ever made in favour of the cause of the provinces. I shall not weary the House with the extracts from the conclusions reached by the delegates to the convention of 1887 ; let it suffice to say that these resolutions constitute one of the historical documents which will ever be read with interest by those who are concerned with the question of provincial autonomy. From the many public actions with which Mr. Mercier's name remains identified, this conference will be handed down to posterity as the most important act of his political record.
For reasons which it would be idle to review at this remote period, the conference of 1887 was barren of immediate results : but, as I said, (he remoter the date of that event, the greater the importance of the resolutions then adopted.
The conference which was held in December, 1902, was but a partial revival of the proceedings of 1887 ; but, as I shall soon explain, the resolutions which were passed at that meeting of premiers are of the utmost importance.
I am happy to say that those two conventions held in 1887 and in 1902 met together,

owing to the action taken l>y the Quebec government It was according to the fitness of things that my native province which was the ' constituante ' of confederation, should take the lead of that movement in favour of provincial autonomy and should promote through temperate and well conducted debates, the establishment of relations, both more fair and more just, between tlie central power and the various provinces. The position taken by the government of the province of Quebec in December last is all the more justifiable as the two administrations which have succeeded each other in power since 1897, under the leadership of the regretted Mr. Marchand and under the present leadership of Mr. Parent, have administered public affairs with an eye to the most rigid economy. As a matter of fact, it is no idle boasting to say that, since 1897, owing to the generous cooperation of all concerned, in our province, we have succeeded in putting a stop to the era of deficits and effected an equilibrium between income and expenditure. How is this fact to be accounted for if not from the increase in population in large cities like Montreal and Quebec '! Owing to their growth as seaports, these cities receive every year a large floating population, and this surplus of population necessarily involves additional expenditure in the administration of justice, and more particularly of the courts of criminal jurisdiction. It is still within the vivid recollection of old practitioners that, not so very long ago, there were only two sessions of the criminal court held in the cities of Quebec and Montreal every year. Before you left the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I was explaining the cause of the increase in some expenditures incurred for some branches of provincial administration. I wish now to call the attention of the House to the glaring disproportion between the revenue derived from the federal treasury and the revenue which the province itself has levied for the administration of public affairs. The following figures show that in that respect, the provinces have done their large share. Of course, I am referring here to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. In 1870, Quebec was drawing from the Dominion treasury a grant of $859,626. In 1901-02, that subsidy amounted to $1,279,105, or an increase of $419,479.
Let us now take the revenue which has been created by the province itself, as the revenue derived from the Crown lands. In 1870 the revenue derived from the land sales was $501,478, while in 1902, it was $1,291,111, or an increase of $788,633. The licenses which in 1870 yielded $98,050, gave $681,229 in 1902. As will be seen, the revenue from this source has increased fivefold since that time, other sources of revenue have been created in order to meet the requirements of the provincial administration. The taxation levied on commercial corporations which did not exist prior to 1870 has yielded $231,695 in 1902, and the duties on successions $222,763. In other words, whereas the Dominion grant has increased from 1870 to 1902 by $419,479, on the other hand, the revenue which the province has derived from its own resources has increased by $4,827,261.
Let us now take the case of the province of Ontario. The figures which I am giving *here are borrowed from a most exhaustive memorandum recently prepared by the Hon. Mr. Ross, Prime Minister of the great sister province. The total revenue of the province of Ontario is $4,466,043. The Dominion grant is $1,339,287. The revenue derived from provincial sources reach $3,126,756.
Now, in the face of such figures, can it be denied that the provinces have done their large share outside of any aid received from the 'Dominion government 7 Can it be denied that the provinces, by means of contributions levied upon the taxpayers, have drawn from local sources, enormous sums of money to meet the expenditure of their Mr. LEMIEUX (Gaspe).
administration ? Have they not unmercifully taxed themselves to meet their engagements ? Of course the expenditure has considerably increased. In 1870 the grants to public education in the province of Quebec, amounted to $279,972, while in 1902, they reached $469,184. Whereas the expenditure of the Department of Agriculture amounted to $49,863 in 1870, it rose to $119,683 in 1902. For the same departments in the province of Ontario, the outlay for public education was $247,192 in 1801, and $782,193 in 1901, whereas for agriculture, the expenditure was $56,211 in 1861, and $209,258 in 1901. Now, I appeal to the hon. gentlemen who sit on both sides of the House, whether there is a single man who would dare to hold, at this stage of our history, that we should apply the brakes to such cases as public education and agriculture, instead of giving them a new impetus, and such remarkable development as is seen nowadays in other parts of the world ? Why, Sir, does it not stand to reason that these are outlays which are bound to increase in proportion to the very growth of population ? In these modern days, public education, as we all know, is becoming more and more expensive. Our institutions insist upon higher salaries being paid, and rightly so ; and competition makes it necessary for arts and manufactures to be up to the standard of modern science. Again, the new conditions of agriculture require more skill and greater technical knowledge. To recoil from an increased expenditure would be tantamount to saying that provinces must remain at a standstill.
But, Sir, whereas on the one hand, the grant which we receive from the Dominion exchequer is fixed and unalterable, on the other hand, the sources of revenue which the provinces have handed over to the Dominion have trebled in value. Let us take the customs and the excise. In 1867-68, the income from those sources was $11,580,968.25, whereas in 1901, it reached $38,245,223, or an increase of $26,664,254.75. Now, in 1867, the total subsidies received from the Dominion government by the provinces amounted to $2,753,966, or 24 per cent of the revenue of which they had divested themselves, whereas in 1901, the subsidies jiaid over to the provinces were $4,250,607, or 11 per cent only of the same revenue. Moreover, there is this remarkable anomaly, that the increase of population in the various provinces involves the creation of fresh sources of expenditure, which are beyond the control of the men of power, whereas from that same cause the Dominion government derives a fresh source of revenue which cannot fail to develop more and more. The question is, how is this anomalous position to be remedied, which impresses every thoughtful man who is anxious about the lawful claims of the provinces ? For my part I am of opinion

that in the demands set forth by the interprovincial conference in December last, is to be found the true and practical remedy to the existing difficulties. The wording of those resolutions is very clear and very explicit:

Instead of an annual grant per head of population now allowed, the annual payment hereafter to be at the same rate of eighty cents per head, but on the population of the province as ascertained from time to time by the last decennial census, until such population exceeds 2,500,000 ; and at the rate of sixty cents per head for so much of said population as may exceed 2,500,000.
As I said a little while ago, such a demand seems fair and reasonable. The provinces, of their own accord, did delegate certain powers to the central government and did hand over to them the best of their revenue. Is it reasonable to believe that the idea of the fathers of confederation should have been that such a renunciation of powers and such a transfer of revenue should work to the detriment of the provinces, by placing them for ever in straitened circumstances, bordering upon poverty ?
The federalists think that the remedy to that state of affairs is to be found in the power of self-taxation and in the borrowing power, which the provinces have preserved. But such an argument no longer holds, in view of the enormous burdens shouldered by the provinces since 1867. The people in the province of Quebec at least, are opposed to dircet taxation and to any further loans. Moreover, as to the parcelling out of the public domain, that is a policy which all right-minded people, all patriotic men antagonize. It is our children's patrimony and their future is intimately linked to it. It would be unfair to deprive our fellow countrymen of the public lands and the natural resources they contain, for the benefit of aliens and speculators who have no permanent interests in this country.
We do not want the provinces to be a mere geographical expression in this Dominion of ours. Any attempt to build up the central power at the expense of the provinces ought to be discountenanced. To call this demand for better terms a raid on the federal treasury is no argument at all. When the federal government grants every
year to powerful corporations subsidies amounting to millions of dollars, do not they feel that the position of the provinces is growing more and more humiliating '! Why should the provinces have to play the part of paupers, when they represent in this country interests far more important than the interests of the great corporations referred to 1 Do you not think it would be a better policy to settle once for all, by means of a mutual understanding, the financial status of the provincial legislatures, so as to put a stop, for the future, to repeated demands for better terms ? A sad spectacle this House has been a witness to, within the last twenty-five years. Of course, to quote a sensible saying, it is the people who pay ; but it is also the same people who contribute millions to an overflowing public exchequer. It is no use quibbling here. The taxpayers in the various provinces are also the taxpayers of the central government. The additional sums which will be paid to the provinces by the Dominion government will be expended on agriculture, colonization and public education ; and after all, it is Canada that will benefit by them. An increase in the Dominion subsidies to the provinces is necessary, I may even say, it is imperative. From the very inception of confederation, a progressive increase in the revenue of the provinces should have been provided for, on the basis of a subsidy adjustable to the increase of [DOT]population. Suppose that the population of the province of Quebec should receive an increase of one million within the next twenty years ; will any man, in his sober senses, pretend that the federal subsidy should continue for all time to come, to be determined on the original basis of the population of 1861 ? The question admits of no doubt. Therefore, it is necessary that there should be a fairer redistribution of income and expenditure. Let us bear in mind that the conditions in Canada have greatly changed since 1867. From the necessity of keeping pace with modern progress, from the development of our resources and the new needs of the country as well as the requirements of competition, fresh duties have devolved upon provincial governments which it would be idle to postpone any longer. As to the charges of extravagance brought against the provinces, I may say that they are worthless ; because, it stands to reason that when the provinces have aided in the building of great railway lines, and have opened up to settlement tracts of uncultivated lands, they have thereby notably contributed to the increase of population ; they have also increased tenfold the volume of general trade, and promoted, to a large extent, the development of the whole country. It would be, indeed, a very poor policy, quite at variance with sound political economy, to add to the embarrassed circumstances of the provinces, in proportion to the general development of the

country. Take away from the provinces the assistance they are entitled to, and you thereby deprive them of the best incentive to self-development. As I said last year, the'provinces exist, true enough, but they barely live under the present condition of affairs. They are entitled to something more than a bare existence ; they have a right to live.
Motion agreed to.

MCLENNAN (Inverness) moved for:	*
Copies of all correspondence, Orders in Council, and other papers, in connection with the prosecution, by the Customs Department, for the scuttling of the schooner ' Euxine,' of Mar-garee Island, while reported on a smuggling expedition, from St. Pierre, Miquelon.

With regard to the motion, 1 do not know exactly what action the department took in the matter and how the case actually stands. It seems that all the [DOT] papers are not available, but whatever papers can be had will be brought down. This is a case which occurred under the late government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS (Hon. Win. Paterson).

speechtext: It did occur some years ago, under the regime of the late administration, and seems to have hung fire somewhere between the departments and the-courts. For some years nothing was done and the case stood in abeyance until a repetition of this species of illicit traffic in recent years caused public opinion to become alive to the importance of stamping it down. The proximity of the island of St. Pierre, Miquelon to Cape Breton has facilitated smuggling operations between the two places, and it is therefore of great urgency that offenders should be taught to respect the law. In order to' do this, it is considered advisable to start in with the original offender and have this case pushed to the end. Hence it is that I call for the papers at present. The prosecution was entered into by the Customs Department under the late government, but it would seem that a very important witness on that occasion conveniently disappeared, which for the time set the case at rest, but it appears that in recent years evidence has become available which is calculated to throw some light upon this mysterious matter, and public opinion calls for a further probing of the case. I believe that important evidence which was not available on the first occasion is available now, and I hope that the department will take the case up where it seems to have dropped. When last heard of. I believe it was in the hands of the agent of the Department of Justice at that time in Halifax. Who that gentleman is I cannot recall, but the papers are in that office now and should be available. While I agree with the lion.
minister that all the papers may not be available in his department, I shall be glad, if all those which are, should be brought down.
Motion agreed to.

MACLEAN (East York) moved second reading of Bill (No. 4) respecting telephone companies. He said:	This Bill
is. substantially the Bill introduced last session and it is of great public interest. I have discussed it very fully on previous occasions both in the House and in the Committee. And it is a Bill that demands passage now more than ever. It is altogether in the public interest, and will go a long way to promote commerce and communication. I do not intend, at the present time, to discuss it very fully, but I expect from the government to-night a statement of their intention with regard to the matter. Last session, when I introduced the Bill, the Minister of Justice, on behalf of the government, said it was the intention of the government to introduce a Bill dealing with the question. And he did introduce a Bill which came before the committee; and then the statement was made in the committee that the questions involved were of such a character that it would take a year to consider them fully. That year has elapsed. I have asked the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) if it was the intention of the government to redeem its pledge and bring in a Bill this session. So far, I have not had an answer to that question. I am quite willing to give the leader of the House (Hon. Sir William Mulock) an opportunity to say now whether it is the intention of the government to bring in that Bill.

I was going to make a suggestion. Whether or not the government brings in a Bill, that circumstance would not be a good reason for not inviting the attention to this question. It is a very large question. The Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines is a large committee, comprising about three-fifths or, perhaps, three-quarters of the members of the House, and perhaps a better plan would be to let this go to the committee and have a thorough discussion there. The government and the House will then be better able to give an opinion on the subject.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speechtext: But a government must redeem its pledges.
Oil, no.

Well, some of us. take tliat view. A solemn pledge lias been given to tbe people that we shall have a Telephone Bill this session. Deputations have been here and interviewed the government. The Minister of Justice said that he was giving all the attention he could to the constitutional question that had arisen. And I expect that Bill, and the country expects it. But the leader of the House tells us that he lias no policy to announce and does not know what the intention of the government is
I did not say anything of the kind.

Well, the hon. gentleman was not in a posit ion to give any information on the matter. In all fairness, in view of the large issues that come up in connection with the question, a public statement ought to he made by the government with regard to it . But I am in the hands of the government, and I must go to the Committee with the Bill, fight it out there and then come back to the House, if necessary. There is only one change in my Bill from last session. While a number have raised the issue in this House that the Bill I introduced interfered with municipal rights, I never admitted that it did so, as at first drafted; but, to provide for that point, I have inserted a clause that any rights gi'anted to the telephone companies under the charter of this Act are subject to the rights of municipalities. But I am not dealing with the constitutional question I am dealing with a practical public grievance. A telephone monopoly exists in this country, and ail I ask is that the telephone business be put on a competitive basis, that anybody and everbody may go into telephone business and that the well known principles of the law be applied to telephone business as to any other. So I have made the necessary provision regarding municipal rights. I intend to go on with the Bill. I am ready to go to the Committee; and. with that understanding, I move the second reading and that the Bill be sent to the Committee.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

MACLEAN (East York) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 5) to amend the Railway Act. He said : This is a very short Bill. It deals with one phase of the telephone grievance in this country. That grievance has developed since last session. When a year's grace was given to the Bell
Telephone Company they went out and made contracts with all the railway companies in Canada, and so they secured a telephone monopoly in all the railroad stations in the country. I contend that this is against public policy. The railroads of this country should be given facilities with regard to telephones, as they are compelled by the Railway Act to give equal facilities in their transportation of freight. This Bill is a very short amendment to secure that end. I should like to see the hon. member (Mr. Dyment) who represents Fort William and Port Arthur in his place to-night that he might tell us what is going on in those two progressive towns. The people in these towns have organized a municipal telephone service for the two towns. They are giving the people a better telephone service than the Bell Telephone Company gave, and charging only half its price. But they find, under this invidious agreement between the telephone companies and the railways, that the public telephone systems of these towns are debarred from entering the Canadian Pacific Railway station. And representatives of the people of Port Arthur and Fort William are here to-day in Ottawa to ask that the amendment that I now propose or some similar amendment may pass. In my riding of East York, the farmers-and I hope the farming members of the House will listen to me, and I hope the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) who comes from that county is listening to me, and I hope the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Ross) is in his place and listening to me-the farmers of East York, and of Pickering in South Ontario, could not get telephone connection. They implored the Bell Telephone Company to give it to them. An immense price was demanded. I have to pay $180 a year for my telephone service in the township of York. I find the service useful, and I have to pay the price. A veterinary half a mile away was asked $1G0 for a telephone service. But he cannot pay it, and is not able to answer his calls. This, of course, is a great inconvenience. All the doctors there were held up in the same way. But the farmers had enough spirit to organize an independent telephone system. They organized it on the basis of each man paying $40 as an initial payment; and an annual contribution of $5. On this basis they made first-class telephone service which they own and control themselves. Eighteen went into the first line. But they wished to have connection with the Locust Hill station of the Canadian Pacific Railway. But when they went there, they were told:	Gentlemen, we cannot let the farmers' line into the station because of the exclusive agreement we gave to the Bell Telephone Company last year. I wired to Sir Thomas Shaughnessy about it, and he was willing to give the farmers the service if he could get out of his agreement with the Bell Telephone Company. Who were

these farmers who applied to get access by telephone to the station ? Every one of them was a customer of the Canadian Pacific Railway and all they wished was the privilege of being able to ask the Canadian Pacific Railway agent whether the trains were on time, whether their freight had arrived, and questions of that character which the railway' people are only too pleased to answer, if you knock at their door-but if you wish to get in through a hole in the wall by a telephone wire, you have to ask the consent of the Bell Telephone Company. This is an iniquitous state of affairs, contrary to public policy. It is contrary to the political principles of both parties, and is a thing that ought to be stopped. All that my Bill does is to insist on every railway company giving equal telephone facilities to every one who asks for them. I would like to know where the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) is to-night and whether he is prepared to make a statement on this subject. Here are two Bills relating to the branch of affairs Which he is supposed to administer, and he is not here to give us an answer to our questions. The hon. member for Victoria,N.S., spoke about the sessional gaieties the other evening. Apparently the sessional gaieties are taking up the time of the ministers, for they are not here to state the policy of the government on public questions. The farmers of Canada, from one end to the other are watching this little Bill, and they expect some kind of declaration with regard to it. I suppose that all the information I shall get is that I must go to the Committee. But what is the intention of the government ?
Now, I would not have spoken so warmly on this point if I had not had a large experience of being jollied, as the term is, in committees in regard to these public Bills that I have introduced. I intend now to insist on some kind of fair treatment of these measures and some kind of statement from the government as to what they intend to do. They need not answer me if they don't wish to, but I will try the best way I know how to take care of these Bills and get a full discussion of them. I trust the House to-night will send this Bill on to the committee, and I trust further, in view of all the agitation in the country, and in view of the interest the farmers are taking on this question, that I will have the assistance of the government in passing both these Bills, especially this very short one. I am not exceeding my right in expecting that the ministers having charge of these important questions should be in their places and prepared to state the policy of the government in regard to them.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

Mr. JAMES CLANCY (Bothwell) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 15) to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1900. He said : This is the same Bill I introduced on two former occasions. The object of the Bill is to amend the Dominion Elections Act so as to prevent what is now a most insidious and dangerous form of intimidation. I regret that I have to say it, and I say it with a feeling of shame, that in the province of Ontario we have not a secret ballot, and that is well known from one end of the province to the other. Though we have a secret ballot in the Dominion Act, it is well understood by those who know anything about these matters that when an election comes on men are intimidated and are told that the Dominion ballot is not secret, and they had better be very careful how they vote because it will be discovered. The object of this Bill is to make such a threat an offence against the Election Act, and to make it punishable and liable to the penalties that attend the usual acts of corruption. I do not think that I need spend any more time in urging the necessity of a Bill of this kind.

I think there is some misunderstanding. The Minister of Justice, who has these matters in charge, is not here tonight, and I would be glad if the hon. gentleman would allow his Bill to stand over. The minister had an impression that these Bills would not be reached to-night, otherwise he would have made some arrangement about them. So if the hon. gentleman has no objection to let it stand over, it will come up on the first order the next day.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: I may inform the Minister of Finance that the Minister of Justice has already had that stand over on two occasions in order that he might take it to the block and use his hatchet. I want to say to the hon. gentleman that it is just as well that he should know my position. I do not intend that the Minister of Justice shall dispose of that Bill at this session without a vote of this House. I will accept the proposition made by the Minister of Finance on the understanding that the Bill shall not lose its place, and shall become the first order of the day.

When I say the first order-there are very few orders ahead of it. I do not make the suggestion with any intention of preventing a vote. There are only two or three motions ahead of it. and as we are at the beginning of the session, there is not the least danger that the matter will not come up again at an early date.
Motion withdrawn.
